summary: The note examines the cybersecurity threat to power grids, using a November 13, 2023 cyberattack that blacked out Charleston, West Virginia as its central case. It explains how attacks exploit SCADA control systems and IoT devices, and describes defenses including layered technical measures, AI/ML monitoring, the Grid Cybersecurity Act, public-private partnerships and consumer awareness. It concludes that grid cybersecurity requires ongoing vigilance and cross-sector collaboration.
one_line: Overview of power grid cyber threats, anchored by the November 2023 Charleston blackout, and the technology, policy, partnership and consumer measures used to defend grids.
key_facts: On Monday, November 13, 2023, a cyberattack on its power grid caused a comprehensive blackout in Charleston, West Virginia, darkening traffic lights and halting businesses.
Rachel Nguyen, a local cybersecurity expert, revealed that the Charleston attackers deployed malware via a phishing scheme that infiltrated the network of the Charleston Power Utility.

Johnathan Haines, a cybersecurity engineer with the Federal Electric Reliability Corporation (FERC), said grid cyberattacks are moving "from mere nuisances to potential catalysts of widespread infrastructure collapse."

Grid generation, transmission and distribution are coordinated by SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) control systems, which adversaries exploit to disrupt communications, send malicious commands or damage physical components that can take weeks or months to repair.
At a UN summit on September 27, 2023, Swedish delegate Lars Svensson said "power grid security is international security. A hit on one is a hit on all."
A major grid attack could compromise hospital operations, halt city water supply due to electric pumps, and take critical internet data centers offline.
After the Charleston incident, the note says Internet of Things devices such as smart thermostats and solar panel connections were seen to widen the entry points for cyber threats.
Miles Turner, CISO at ElectricGrid Security Inc., recommends a layered approach: secure-by-design principles, rigorous penetration testing, employee training and a robust incident response plan.
AI and ML systems are increasingly deployed to monitor grid operations for anomalies that could signify a cyber intrusion.

The Grid Cybersecurity Act, passed on December 1, 2023, mandates real-time threat sharing between utilities and federal oversight bodies and sets a framework for coordinated incident response, according to analyst Diana Perkins.
On February 8, 2024, Homeland Security's Cyber Emergency Response Team (CERT) and multiple electric utilities jointly quashed an attempted cyber incursion that could have impacted multiple states.
Elena Rodriguez, director of community outreach at SecurePower, stressed empowering customers to recognize and report suspicious activities as part of the cybersecurity ecosystem.
